passage:
Teacher's note, Class 4, Tuesday. At recess Baljeet stood alone by the water tank, turning a pebble in his hand. He has done this for a week. I was about to step in when Payal, running out with the football, stopped. “We need a goalkeeper. Baljeet, want to be it?” No speech, no fuss. Baljeet's face changed. He ran to the goalpost and stayed there all recess, shouting “Save!” once so loudly that everyone laughed, kindly.

What I did next: I stayed back and let them play. In the afternoon I quietly asked Payal what made her ask. “He looked like he wanted to,” she said. I'll keep mixing the football teams each week.

qa.q: Where was Baljeet standing alone at recess?
qa.a: Baljeet stood alone by the water tank, turning a pebble in his hand.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have felt when Payal asked to be the goalkeeper?
qa.a: Baljeet probably felt surprised and glad to be wanted, shown by the change in Baljeet's face and the loud shout.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make at recess, and why might it help?
qa.a: The teacher stayed back and let the children play, so the invitation stayed ordinary and unforced.

qa.q: What might Payal have been thinking when asking Baljeet?
qa.a: Payal saw that Baljeet looked as if Baljeet wanted to play and simply acted on it, with no big plan.

grounding: A child invites a lone child into a game without fuss, and a teacher's note records how it changed the school day for the one included.

passage:
Monday. At recess we were playing a running game, me, Sneha, Ruchi and two others. Tejas was sitting by the tree again, drawing in the dust with a stick. I don't know why I did it, but I called, “Tejas, we need one more! Come!” Ruchi shrugged. Sneha said, “Okay.” Tejas looked up as if he thought I was talking to someone else. Then he ran over so fast he tripped, and everyone laughed, the nice kind. He was really good at being the catcher. At the bell he said “Thanks” very quietly.

Tomorrow I'm going to call him again.
— Afreen

qa.q: What was Tejas doing by the tree?
qa.a: Tejas was drawing in the dust with a stick.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when Afreen called him to join the game?
qa.a: Tejas felt surprised and eager, looking up as if the call were meant for someone else and then running over so fast he tripped.

qa.q: What small choice did Afreen make that changed Tejas's recess?
qa.a: Afreen called out that they needed one more and invited Tejas without fuss.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt when Tejas said "Thanks" very quietly at the bell?
qa.a: Afreen probably felt pleased and glad about calling Tejas over, which is why Afreen plans to call Tejas again tomorrow.

grounding: A child invites a lone child into a recess game without fuss, and a small act of inclusion changes the day.

passage:
In the village school ground near Nashik, the kho-kho game was already running when Siddharth, the new boy from the city, came out. He stood by the babul tree, holding his water bottle, watching.
Sunaina noticed. She didn't make a speech. She just ran over between rounds. “We need one more on our side. Come.”
Siddharth blinked. “I don't know the rules properly.”
“Just sit when I tap you and run when you're tapped,” she said, and pulled him into the line.
He was slow the first time and fast the second. By the last round, he was laughing with the others, dust on his knees. On the way back to class, two boys asked him where he was from.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth stand when he came out?
qa.a: He stood by the babul tree, holding his water bottle.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt when Sunaina said "Come"?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and a bit nervous, but relieved to be invited into the game.

qa.q: What did Sunaina's invitation do well?
qa.a: It was quick and ordinary, with no fuss, and gave Siddharth a simple way to join straight away.

qa.q: How might the two boys see Siddharth after the game?
qa.a: They seem curious and friendly, now seeing him as part of the group.

grounding: Shows a child inviting a lone new boy into a game without fuss, a small act that changes his school day.

passage:
At break in their school in Amsterdam, the girls' skipping rope was going fast. Tariq, who had arrived from Syria three weeks earlier, sat on the bench, watching the rope swing.
Nadia was holding one end. When the next girl tripped, she called out, “Tariq! Can you hold this end? My arm is tired.”
Tariq looked around, not sure she meant him. Then he came over and took the rope.
He turned it too fast at first, and everyone laughed, and so did he. After a few minutes Nadia said, “Your turn to jump.” He jumped seven times before tripping.
When the bell rang, Tariq walked back inside next to Nadia, talking about football.

qa.q: How many times did Tariq jump before tripping?
qa.a: He jumped seven times before tripping.

qa.q: How did Tariq feel when he looked around, not sure she meant him?
qa.a: He felt unsure and surprised, not used to being asked to join.

qa.q: Why was asking Tariq to hold the rope a clever way to include him?
qa.a: It was a small, practical request, so he could join without feeling singled out or pitied.

qa.q: How might the girls who laughed have seen Tariq?
qa.a: They seemed friendly, laughing with him, not at him, and happy to have another player.

grounding: Shows a child inviting a lone newcomer into a skipping game without fuss, changing his school day.

passage:
In the community centre's games room, the carrom board was always taken by the same four. Vishal, who came every Saturday since his family moved into the chawl, usually sat by the window with a comic he'd already read.
Hansa looked up from the board. “Vishal, we need a partner. Rohit has to leave early.”
Vishal hesitated. “I'm not very good.”
“Nobody is, except Rohit,” said Hansa. “Sit.”
He sat. He missed his first shot, then pocketed a white one. Hansa clapped. “See?”
By five o'clock, he was arguing about the rules like everyone else. When he left, the centre supervisor noticed he said “bye” to all four, not just to her.

qa.q: What did Vishal usually sit with?
qa.a: A comic he'd already read.

qa.q: How did Vishal seem to feel when he said "I'm not very good"?
qa.a: He seemed nervous and unsure, worried about joining a group that always played together.

qa.q: What made Hansa's invitation effective?
qa.a: Hansa gave a practical reason, brushed off his worry lightly, and made him part of the game without any fuss.

qa.q: How might the centre supervisor see the change in Vishal?
qa.a: The supervisor seems pleased and touched, noticing he now says bye to all four.

grounding: Shows a child inviting a lone boy into a carrom game without fuss, a small act that changes his day.

passage:
I'm Lokesh, and I sit by the window, so I see everything at break.
A new girl, Farah, spent her whole first week standing by the water cooler. Nobody was mean. Nobody asked her either.
On Monday we were one short for kho-kho. Deepika walked to the cooler and said, "We need one more. Want to be on my side?" No big speech. Farah nodded so fast her plait bounced.
She got caught twice at first. Deepika just said, "Run zig-zag," and tagged her in again.
By Wednesday Farah was shouting "Kho!" louder than any of us. I don't know what Farah was thinking that first day at the cooler, but she hasn't stood there since.

qa.q: Where did Farah stand during her first week?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: How did Farah seem to feel when Deepika invited her?
qa.a: Farah seemed excited and relieved, nodding so fast her plait bounced.

qa.q: What made Deepika's invitation work so well?
qa.a: It was simple and ordinary, with no fuss, and Deepika kept encouraging her after she got caught.

qa.q: How might Deepika see what she did?
qa.a: Deepika probably saw it as nothing special, since the team just needed one more, without realising how much it changed Farah's week.

grounding: Shows a child inviting a lone new classmate into a game without fuss, and how that small act changes her school days.
